text: Almost every broken-deployment ticket says something vague, like "can't connect" or "doesn't work." But in real environments, the actual cause almost always turns out to be one of just five things. This lesson lays out that short list, so you're checking a known set of suspects instead of guessing from scratch, the same way this path has already made you debug twice.

First, network and routing — a resource in the wrong subnet, or a missing route to the gateway, which was the entire root cause behind Lesson 31's unreachable instance. Second, security group or NSG rules, too tight, too loose, or simply stale, like the office IP range that moved in Lesson 32. Third, DNS resolution — an old IP left behind after a resource was recreated, a private zone that was never linked to the right VNet, or a typo'd hostname that resolves to nothing instead of erroring loudly.

Fourth, IAM or RBAC permission gaps — a managed identity or user role missing the one permission a new feature now depends on, which looks exactly like a broken resource until you actually read the error text. Fifth, a resource quota or limit quietly hit, like a vCPU ceiling, an IP address limit, or an API rate limit, which fails a deployment or a scaling event with no obvious configuration error anywhere to find, especially on newer accounts that haven't requested an increase.

You've already lived two of these. Lesson 31's meridian-web2 instance couldn't be reached because it launched into the wrong subnet with no public IP at all — place number one, network and routing. Lesson 32's new VM hung on SSH because an NSG rule still pointed at an office's old IP range after an office move — place number two, a stale security rule. Same vague symptom both times; two very different, very specific root causes.

These five aren't a random grab bag: they're the layers a request actually passes through, roughly in the order traffic travels — network, firewall rule, name resolution, identity, and capacity. That's also the order this path built them in, chapter by chapter. Lessons 26 and 27 turn the first four into full, repeatable diagnostic sequences you can run on a real incident, starting with connectivity failures next.
